title: Kiosk vs phone ordering for restaurants
seoTitle: Kiosk vs phone ordering for restaurants
description: Compare kiosk and phone ordering for restaurants. See where each works best, what it costs, and how to choose for rush hours.
question: Should I use kiosks or phone ordering in my restaurant?
answer: Kiosks work well for walk-in guests who are already at the counter, while phone ordering works better for callers who want pickup or delivery without waiting in line. Many restaurants use both: kiosks for in-store ordering and an AI phone host like ROAL for answering calls, taking orders, and sending clean tickets to the kitchen.
summary: You’ll be able to choose the right ordering setup for your counter, phone, and kitchen.
intro:
Kiosk vs phone ordering usually comes down to where your guests are standing. Kiosks help when people are already in the restaurant. Phone ordering helps when customers are calling from home, work, or the road.

For many independent restaurants, the best answer is not either/or. It is matching the tool to the job. A kiosk can speed up the front counter. A phone host like ROAL can take pickup and delivery orders, answer menu questions, and send the order to the kitchen screen without tying up your staff.

sections.h2: What problem does each option solve?
sections.body:
A kiosk solves in-store lines. A phone host solves ringing phones. If your counter is crowded, a kiosk lets guests place an order without repeating it to staff. If your phone rings during lunch or dinner, an AI phone host can answer, take the order, and give a ready time.

Here is the simple split many owners use:
- **Kiosk:** walk-in customers, counter orders, add-ons at the register
- **Phone ordering:** pickup orders, delivery orders, menu questions, hours, address, parking
- **Staff:** reservations, catering, allergy-sensitive questions, complaints, manager requests

Example script line for phone ordering: "Thanks for calling. I can take your pickup order now, or I can answer a menu question first."

If you are comparing phone options, [AI phone host vs online ordering](/compare/online-ordering) and [AI phone host vs answering service](/compare/answering-service) are useful side-by-side reads.

sections.h2: Which one is easier for guests to use?
sections.body:
Kiosks are easiest for guests who are already in front of them and want to move fast. Some people like the screen because they can tap extras, see items, and review their cart before paying. But a kiosk only helps the person standing in your store.

Phone ordering works for guests who are not in the restaurant yet. That matters for takeout spots, pizza shops, delis, and family restaurants where people still prefer to call. ROAL reads the live menu, takes items, sizes, modifiers, and notes, then confirms the order back on the call.

A quick owner checklist:
1. Do most of your orders start with a phone call?
2. Do people line up at the counter during lunch or dinner?
3. Do you need help with hours, address, or menu questions after staff gets busy?
4. Do you have enough space for a kiosk without blocking the line?

If your answer to 1 or 3 is yes, phone ordering deserves a hard look.

sections.h2: What does each option cost in real restaurant terms?
sections.body:
The cost difference matters more than the device itself. Kiosks often mean hardware, setup, and upkeep. Phone ordering tools are often priced as monthly software, human answering billed by the minute or call, or delivery apps that take a commission from each order.

Here is a simple way to compare, using example numbers you can swap for your own:

| Option | Typical cost shape | What to ask yourself |
|---|---|---|
| Kiosk | Device + maintenance | How many walk-in orders will use it each day? |
| Human answering | Per minute or per call | How busy are your phone peaks? |
| Monthly phone tool | Fixed monthly fee per location | What if call volume is light this month? |
| ROAL | $0.90 per completed phone order | How many confirmed phone orders do you expect? |

Say you get 200 completed phone orders in a month. At $0.90 each, that would be $180 for those orders. Plug in your own volume and compare it with any fixed monthly fee you are paying now. ROAL has no monthly fee, no setup fee, and no per-minute fee, and calls and test calls are free.

sections.h2: How do kiosks and phone ordering affect your staff?
sections.body:
A kiosk can reduce counter back-and-forth, but it does not answer the phone. If your staff is already juggling prep, the register, and takeout bags, the ringing phone still pulls them away. That is where phone ordering often wins for small teams.

Phone ordering also helps with the messy calls that staff do not want to stop for, such as:
- menu questions
- hours and address questions
- parking questions
- reservation requests
- catering inquiries
- allergy-sensitive questions
- complaints and manager requests

ROAL can handle the first group and hand the harder calls to staff with a summary. That means your team gets the details without having to repeat the whole conversation.

A practical phone-hand-off script for staff: "Thanks, I see the summary. I’ll take it from here."

For owners short on staff, [short-staffed shifts](/use-cases/short-staffed) is a good match to this problem.

sections.h2: Which one is better for pickup and delivery orders?
sections.body:
For pickup and delivery, phone ordering is usually the better fit. Guests already expect to call, ask a question, or place a quick order while they are on the move. A kiosk does not help there unless the customer is physically in your store.

ROAL is built for those live calls. It can take items, sizes, modifiers, and notes from the restaurant’s menu, collect the caller’s name and phone, quote a ready time, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. It also speaks the caller’s language and will not offer items marked sold out.

Worked example:
- Say your average phone order is $28.
- Say you get 120 completed phone orders in a month.
- That is 120 orders billed at $0.90 each, or $108.

Now compare that to the time your team spends answering calls during lunch and dinner. If you also use [Phone orders vs delivery apps](/compare/delivery-apps), you can see why many owners keep phone ordering in-house instead of sending those orders through a marketplace.

sections.h2: How should I decide if I need one, the other, or both?
sections.body:
A simple decision rule works well for most independent restaurants:

1. Choose a kiosk first if your biggest problem is in-store line speed.
2. Choose phone ordering first if your biggest problem is missed calls, pickup orders, or a busy front counter.
3. Use both if you have steady walk-in traffic and steady phone traffic.

If you use both, keep the jobs separate. Let the kiosk help the guest already standing in front of you. Let the phone host help the caller before they arrive. That reduces friction on both sides.

You can also pair this with your current phone setup. ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically, and you can forward your existing number to it all the time, or only when busy or unanswered. If you want to check the carrier steps later, [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes) is a handy reference.

If you want to test a phone-first setup, [build a free test host from your website](/try).

sections.h2: What should I check before I switch?
sections.body:
Before you choose kiosks vs phone ordering, look at the details that actually affect daily service. The right setup should fit your menu, your staff, and your call volume.

Use this quick checklist:
- Do I have a live menu that changes often?
- Do I get phone orders during lunch and dinner?
- Do customers ask for hours, address, or parking on the phone?
- Do I want the kitchen to see clean tickets instead of handwritten notes?
- Do I need staff to handle only the tricky calls?

ROAL reads public menu pages, menu PDFs, or uploaded menus, and the owner can test-call it right in the browser before going live. The owner also chooses the host’s voice and name. Questions it cannot answer go to an inbox, and once you answer them, it remembers.

That makes it easier to start small and adjust as you learn what your guests actually use.

takeaways: Kiosks help with in-store lines; phone ordering helps with callers and pickup orders.
For many restaurants, phone ordering is the better fit for takeout, delivery, and menu questions.
ROAL charges $0.90 per completed phone order, with no monthly fee or per-minute fee.
The best setup is often both: kiosk for the counter, phone host for the line.
Use your own order volume and call volume to compare costs before you switch.

faq.q: Is a kiosk better than phone ordering for a small restaurant?
faq.a: Not always. If most of your business comes from callers, phone ordering usually fits better than a kiosk. If your biggest problem is the line at the counter, a kiosk may help more. Many small restaurants end up using both because they solve different jobs.

faq.q: Can phone ordering replace a kiosk?
faq.a: It can replace a kiosk for phone-based orders, but not for guests standing in your restaurant. A phone host handles pickup and delivery calls, while a kiosk serves walk-in guests. The right answer depends on where most of your orders start.

faq.q: How do I compare kiosk cost with phone ordering cost?
faq.a: Compare the full cost, not just the device price. Kiosks may involve hardware and upkeep, while phone tools may charge a fixed monthly fee, per minute, or per completed order. With ROAL, you can compare against $0.90 per completed phone order and no monthly fee.

faq.q: What happens if the phone host cannot answer a question?
faq.a: ROAL sends those questions to an inbox, and the owner answers once. After that, the phone host knows the answer for future calls. Tricky calls like catering, complaints, allergy-sensitive questions, and manager requests are handed to staff with a summary.
